issues.issue: The date is left blank ("made as of June __, 2004"), so the instrument's effective date cannot be determined from its own face. That is a mechanical omission a court could be asked to fill.
The preamble identifies DMSA as a New Jersey corporation while Schedule A gives it a Pennsylvania address, a minor discrepancy between the preamble and the schedule it incorporates.
"Unless the context otherwise requires" leaves open when a defined meaning yields to context, but the phrase is standard boilerplate.

"Control" is defined as the power to direct management and policies "directly or indirectly ... by contract or otherwise," a boundary that is inherently fact-dependent. Whether a given DMSA-related entity is an "Affiliate" could be argued either way.
Section 10.1(i) requires the books to be kept with "a copy of ... the Certificate," a term never defined, while this definition uses "Articles." The mismatch is trivial but real.

The definition fixes contributions by reference to Section 4.1/Schedule A, and Schedule A records LSB's contribution as the garbled figure "$00,001.00," so the "aggregate amount of money" contributed is not ascertainable. The conflict is with Schedule A as incorporated by Section 4.1(i).

"Covered Person" sweeps in a long chain of persons ending in "any employee or agent of the Company or its Affiliates," and it is not clear whether the Affiliates of a Member's officers are inside or outside the list. The reach of the enumeration is arguable.
Section 17.11 confers rights under the Agreement on no Person "except the Members and Managers," yet this definition underpins the indemnification right in Section 12.4 for a much wider class.

The definition is garbled — "such Member's interest of the profits and losses" and "represents any Member Votes held by a member" — leaving unclear whether an Interest is a unitary bundle or severable economic and voting components. That matters for the transfer provisions.

Clause (iii) makes all "policies, practices and guidelines of any governmental body" a "Law," a general sweep sitting oddly against the specific legal instruments enumerated in (i) and (ii). Its outer reach is uncertain.

"Majority" is defined as "a majority of the Member Votes" while "Majority Vote" means approval by Members holding a majority of Votes; the two near-identical terms are used interchangeably for quorum and for decision. A reader could confuse the presence requirement with the voting requirement.

"Members" is defined as "two (2) or more of such Persons," so the plural term has no referent if only one member remains, yet the Agreement uses "Members" throughout for consent requirements. The definition is capable of an unintended reading.

Member Votes are fixed by Schedule A "as may be amended," while Section 2.1(iii) lets the Secretary update Schedule A and declares such updates not to be amendments — which sits uneasily with Section 17.10's requirement of unanimity for amendments. Voting power could be altered without unanimous consent.

"[A]ny amounts determined by the Members to be necessary to provide a reasonable reserve for working-capital needs or any other contingencies" gives an unbounded discretionary deduction with no standard for "reasonable" or "other contingencies." The size of Net Cash Flow can be argued either way.
The deduction is committed to "the Members," while Section 9.2 commits the timing and amount of all distributions to the Board; the two decision-makers are not reconciled.

The definition simultaneously fixes Percentage Interest "as shown on Schedule A" and "as determined by the unanimous written consent of the Members as adjusted from time to time," leaving unclear which governs if the two diverge.

Section 2.1(iii) empowers the Secretary unilaterally to update Schedule A and says such revisions are not amendments, which cannot be squared with this definition's requirement of unanimous written consent to adjust Percentage Interests.

The definition of "Person" lists "any individual, Company, association ..." using the capitalised defined term "Company," which means Dialogo, LLC itself — an evident mis-capitalisation for "corporation."

Profits and Losses are defined as taxable income under § 703(a), while Section 15.3 distributes on Capital Account balances maintained under Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iv), which requires book rather than tax figures. The two measures are not harmonised.

This clause lets the Secretary update Schedule A and declares such updates not to be amendments, while Schedule A fixes Percentage Interests and Member Votes that the "Percentage Interest" definition and Section 17.10 make alterable only by unanimous consent. The two cannot both stand.

Gerry Pike is directed to file the Articles although he is not a party or a defined role, whereas Section 2.6 assigns comparable filing duties to the Secretary. The allocation of authorised-person duties is inconsistent.

The power to change the registered agent is given to "the Members," while Section 2.6 and Section 2.5 give comparable qualification and location powers to the Board; the Agreement does not say by what vote the Members act here.

The purpose clause states a specific object — "developing Spanish language newspaper(s) and media" — and then a wholly general one, "any lawful act or activity for which limited liability companies may be formed," leaving the scope of "the business" of the Company uncertain. That scope is what fixes the reach of LSB's exclusivity covenant.

Section 12.7 bars LSB from services "to the extent it relates to the business" without defining that phrase, so its content must be drawn from this open-ended purpose clause. The two provisions together leave the covenant's boundary indeterminate.

The broad enumerated powers (e.g. to borrow, to contract, to dispose of assets) are expressed without qualification, while Section 6.8 forbids any of those acts without unanimous Board approval. The relationship between the grant and the restriction is left implicit.

The contributions are fixed by Schedule A, which records LSB's contribution as "$00,001.00" against a 49% Percentage Interest and DMSA's as $50,000 against 51%; the figure is unintelligible and cannot be reconciled with the stated interests.

This section requires any return of Capital Contributions to be made to all Members pro rata to Percentage Interests, while Section 6.8(iii) contemplates distributions "to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions" alone. The two cannot both be given effect.

"[T]he respective invoices of each of DMSA" is garbled — the plural "each of" has no list — so it is unclear whose invoices the Company must pay and on what terms. The exception to the no-compensation rule is therefore indeterminate.

The clause promises Members "profits in accordance with their respective Membership Interests," a term used nowhere else (the defined term is "Percentage Interest"), and it makes profit payment mandatory while Section 9.2 leaves all distributions to the Board's discretion.

"[T]he Members shall be able only to make their capital contributions pursuant to Section 4.1" reads as a prohibition on further contributions, contradicting the second sentence of Section 4.1(ii) permitting additional contributions with unanimous written consent. The wording appears to be a drafting slip.

Section 4.1(ii) expressly permits additional capital contributions with the written consent of all Members, which this clause's "able only to make their capital contributions pursuant to Section 4.1" appears to forbid.

An advance is to be "subject to such terms and conditions acceptable to the Company and each Member," so a loan already made has no ascertainable terms until everyone agrees. The clause creates a debt whose content is left open.

This section gives the Members power "to exercise any and all other rights or powers of the Company" not required to be done by the Board, while Section 6.1 vests management of the business and affairs in the Board "[s]ubject to Section 5.1"; the two provisions define each other circularly.

"[A]ll ordinary and necessary out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Members on behalf of the Company" is a mandatory reimbursement with no cap, approval requirement or definition of "ordinary and necessary." Whether a particular expense qualifies is readily arguable.

Reimbursement here is automatic, while Section 6.8(x) requires unanimous Board approval for contracts with Members and Section 4.3(ii) bars payments to Members save in listed cases. The relationship between the automatic right and those controls is unresolved.

This section forbids a Member to resign before winding up, yet Section 15.2(ii) treats "the ... retirement, resignation, expulsion" of a Member as an event causing dissolution. A resignation cannot both be impossible and be a dissolution trigger.

The second sentence is grammatically broken — special meetings "may be held at such time and place, and shall be stated in the notice" — so it never says who fixes the time and place. The omission matters for the validity of a special meeting.

The clause gives each Member a class-like right to elect its own Directors, yet the "Member" definition states that for Maine Act purposes "the Members shall constitute one (1) class or group of members." The two characterisations pull in different directions.

Special meetings may be called only by the President or at the request of a majority of the Board, so a 49% Member has no way to convene the meeting that Section 5.5 otherwise contemplates for Member action. That leaves the Member-level powers in Section 5.1 without a mechanism.

A quorum is "[a] Majority," i.e. a majority of Member Votes, so DMSA's 51 votes under Schedule A constitute a quorum alone and can transact business without LSB, which is hard to square with the unanimity requirements in Sections 3.2(ii), 13.1 and 17.10.

Written consent by a "Majority" (DMSA alone) can substitute for any meeting action, which sits against Section 17.10's requirement that amendments be executed by all Members and Section 13.1's unanimity for admissions, saved only by the opening "[u]nless otherwise provided."
The section refers to designation as a Manager "for purposes of the Act," a term never defined (the defined term is "Maine Act"). The slip is small but visible on the face of the clause.

Management is vested in the Board "[s]ubject to Section 5.1," while Section 5.1 gives Members all powers not required to be exercised by the Board; neither provision yields, so the locus of authority is genuinely unsettled.

The section excepts actions "otherwise provided in Section 6.9 of this Agreement," but there is no Section 6.9 — the unanimous-approval list is Section 6.8, the numbering having slipped because two sections are numbered 6.6. The cross-reference must be construed to have a referent.

The committee limitation refers to "the actions described in Section 6.9 of this Agreement," but no Section 6.9 exists; the intended reference is evidently Section 6.8. A court would have to supply the referent.

This compensation section is numbered 6.6 and the immediately following removal section is also numbered 6.6, which throws out the numbering relied on by the Section 6.9 cross-references in Sections 6.3 and 6.5.
The section bears the same number, 6.6, as the preceding compensation section, so a reference to "Section 6.6" is ambiguous as between two different subjects.

Clause (iii) carves out of the unanimity requirement "distributions to Members other than to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions," but never says whether that DMSA reimbursement may be made without unanimous approval or is simply outside the list. The carve-out's operation is genuinely unclear.

The DMSA-only capital reimbursement contemplated in clause (iii) cannot be squared with Section 4.3(i), which requires returns of Capital Contributions to be made to all Members in proportion to Percentage Interests and only with the consent of all Members.

Officers are removable by a simple majority of the Board here, while Section 6.8(x) requires unanimous Board approval for "the entering into, amendment or termination of employment contracts with Officers." Removal and termination of the employment contract are not reconciled.

The President is given "general and active management of the business" and authority to execute contracts, while Section 6.8 forbids any Officer to take the listed actions without unanimous Board approval and Section 6.1 vests management in the Board. The scope of unilateral presidential authority is left contestable.
The duty imposed is one "similar to" that of directors of Maine business corporations, a comparative standard that does not say how far the analogy runs. What conduct breaches it is left at large.

This section imposes fiduciary duties of loyalty and care on every Director, while Section 12.7 expressly relieves DMSA of "its fiduciary duties as a Director" for competing ventures; the "[e]xcept to the extent provided herein" opener only partly bridges the gap.
"[T]he same proportions as they shared Interest Profits and Losses" uses "Interest Profits," a term that appears nowhere in Article I; the sentence's measure of sharing is therefore garbled.

Distribution of Net Cash Flow pro rata to Percentage Interests conflicts with Section 6.8(iii), which contemplates distributions "to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions" alone, and with Section 4.3(ii)(a)'s payment of DMSA invoices. The priority among them is not stated.

Timing and amount of distributions are left to the Board here, while the "Net Cash Flow" definition commits the reserve decision to "the Members" and Section 4.3(ii)(b) states that Members "shall be paid profits." Whether any distribution is mandatory is unresolved.

Inspection is permitted "at reasonable times ... for any purpose reasonably related to such Member's interest in the Company," a standard whose boundary invites dispute where a member is alleged to be competing. What counts as a proper purpose is not specified.
The books must be kept with "a copy of ... the Certificate," a term never defined in Article I, which uses "Articles" for the organisational document.

This section requires accrual accounting for determining Profits and Losses, while the "Net Cash Flow" definition requires the cash receipts and disbursements method for the amount actually distributable. The two accounting mandates are not reconciled.

Exculpation turns on acts done "in good faith" and "in a manner reasonably believed to be within the scope of authority," with the carve-out for "gross negligence or willful misconduct" left undefined. Where that line falls is classically contestable.

The exculpation runs in favour of every Covered Person, including a Member, while Section 7.7 imposes corporate-style duties of loyalty and care on Directors and Officers; the interaction of the two standards is not spelled out.

The provision as it appears is a fragment beginning mid-sentence ("professional or expert competence and who has been selected with reasonable care"), with the operative reliance language missing. There is no ascertainable rule to apply.

The section says the Agreement's provisions "replace" other duties "to the extent that they restrict" them, without identifying which provisions do the restricting. Whether common-law fiduciary duties survive is left to argument.

This wholesale replacement of fiduciary duties cannot be squared with Section 7.7, which affirmatively imposes on each Director and Officer the duties of loyalty and care of a Maine business corporation.

Indemnification is promised to every Covered Person, a class far wider than "the Members and Managers," whereas Section 17.11 provides that nothing confers rights under the Agreement on any Person except Members and Managers.

Advancement is mandatory here on a bare undertaking, while Section 6.8(xiv) forbids the incurrence of any material liability or obligation without unanimous Board approval. Whether advancement to a member-litigant needs Board approval is unresolved.
The sentence breaks off at "against any liability that may be asserted," so the scope of the insurance permitted is never completed. The clause cannot be applied as written.

The first sentence is missing words — "and the Company the income or profits derived therefrom" — so it never says what the Company's rights in that income are. The freedom-to-compete grant is unintelligible at its centre.

"DMSA does agree that it intends to use diligent efforts to direct appropriate business to the Company" is a statement of intention rather than a promise, and "appropriate business" and "diligent efforts" are unmeasured. Whether DMSA undertook any enforceable obligation is genuinely arguable.

"LSB shall not provide such services" has no antecedent for "such services," and the covenant is bounded only by "to the extent it relates to the business," a phrase with no definition, duration or geographic limit. What LSB may lawfully do outside the Company turns entirely on construing this sentence.

The clause imposes exclusivity on LSB alone within a section that expressly frees DMSA to compete and relieves it of fiduciary duty, and "the business" must be filled in from Section 3.1's open-ended purpose clause. The asymmetry and the missing referent leave the covenant unreconcilable on its own terms.
DMSA is a Member, not a Director, yet the clause relieves it of "its fiduciary duties as a Director"; whether the relief reaches DMSA's Member duties or its elected Directors' duties is unclear.

Section 7.7 imposes on each Director the fiduciary duties of loyalty and care of a Maine business corporation, and this clause purports to remove them for DMSA; the two provisions point in opposite directions.

Disclosure is barred without "the prior written consent of the LLC," but "LLC" is not a defined term (the entity is "the Company") and the first sentence obliges the parties to keep confidential "all efforts and actions undertaken by them," a scope untethered to the defined Proprietary Information. The obligation's reach is uncertain.

The blanket confidentiality obligation binds DMSA equally, yet Section 12.7 authorises DMSA to pursue competing ventures and to recommend opportunities to others; the two are difficult to operate together.

"Proprietary Information" is defined by a closed list ending in "advertiser provided information, documents and data," with no catch-all and no carve-out for publicly available or independently obtained material. Whether, for example, subscriber contacts already public fall inside is arguable.

Admission requires the approval of all Members here, while Section 16.3 makes a transferee's mere written undertaking to become a party sufficient for a valid transfer and Section 16.8 lets the Board waive transfer restrictions unilaterally. The routes to membership are inconsistent.

The prohibition is circular — no assignment "without complying with the terms of this Agreement" — and does not identify which terms govern assignment. The operative restriction has to be assembled from elsewhere.

A pledge requires the prior written consent of all Members here, while Section 16.8 allows the Board, "[n]otwithstanding anything to the contrary," to waive any transfer restriction in the Agreement. The two cannot both control a pledge.

Clause (ii) makes the "resignation" of a Member a dissolution event, but Section 5.4 provides that a Member may not resign before dissolution and winding up; the trigger cannot occur under the Agreement's own terms.

The direction that "[t]he Members shall continue to distribute Interest Profits and Losses" uses a term found nowhere in Article I and puts the distribution in the Members' hands although the Board conducts the winding up. The sentence is garbled.

Liquidating proceeds go out on Capital Account balances, while Sections 8.1 and 9.1 allocate and distribute on Percentage Interests; with Schedule A recording contributions of $50,000 against $00,001 for a 51/49 split, the two measures produce sharply different outcomes.

Transfers are recorded on Schedule A, which under Section 2.1(iii) the Secretary may update unilaterally without that being an amendment; ownership of record could thus shift without the Member consents Article XVI requires.

"Transfer" is defined to reach involuntary transfers and transfers "by division of marital property or otherwise," while excepting only a revocable proxy; the reach of the "or otherwise" residue against the enumerated specifics is uncertain.

The sanction is that the Interests "will be deemed not to be voted," which cannot be reconciled with Section 5.5(vii)-(viii), where quorum and Majority Vote are computed from the Member Votes fixed by Schedule A. Whether the suspended votes drop out of the denominator is unaddressed.

A transferee becomes a valid holder simply by delivering a written undertaking, whereas Section 13.1 admits new members only "[b]y approval of all of the Members." The Agreement does not say whether such a transferee is a Member.
The section breaks off mid-sentence ("the parties agree that the Company and the other Members shall") and states no waiver rule at all. There is nothing operative to apply.
It applies to transfers "pursuant to Sections 16.9, 16.10, and 16.11 of this Agreement," but Article XVI ends at Section 16.8, so the triggering provisions do not exist in the instrument.

The Board or President may waive the securities-opinion requirement "for good cause," and the opinion must be "in form and substance Satisfactory" to them, with no standard for either judgment. Both phrases are open to competing readings.

The acceptance sentence runs straight into the allocation sentence with no acceptance deadline stated, yet the clause later refers to acceptance not occurring "within the periods set forth above." The missing period makes the mechanism unworkable as written.
The notice must state "the number of LLC Votes to be transferred," a term used nowhere else; the defined term in Article I is "Member Votes."

"Notwithstanding anything to the contrary," the Board may waive any transfer restriction, which nullifies the all-Member consents required by Section 14.3 for pledges and by Section 13.1 for admissions, and the right of first refusal in Section 16.6. A minority Member's protections could be removed by the majority-elected Board.

Notices to the Company go to the address "specified in Section 2.5," which the Board may change at any time, and no method is given for notifying Members of the change. The notice regime is incomplete but workable.

The clause is written backwards: it says failure to insist on performance "shall not prevent a subsequent act ... from having the effect of an original violation," which reads as preserving violations rather than as an anti-waiver rule, and "original violation" is undefined. The sentence's operation is doubtful.

The merger clause supersedes prior agreements only "pertaining to the subject matter hereof," a boundary that decides whether side understandings about LSB's employment or DMSA's services survive. That boundary is regularly fought over.

Maine law is chosen for an entity whose principal place of business is in Massachusetts and whose members are a Massachusetts resident and a New Jersey corporation, which invites argument about the reach of the clause over non-contract claims. The clause itself is clear, however.

Amendments require the affirmative vote and signature of all Members, yet Section 2.1(iii) permits the Secretary to revise Schedule A — which fixes Percentage Interests and Member Votes — and declares that revision not to be an amendment. The unanimity protection can be bypassed.

Rights are confined to "the Members and Managers," which excludes the wider class of Covered Persons expressly given indemnification and expense advancement by Sections 12.4 and 12.5. The two provisions cannot both be given full effect.
